species.name: Megasoma sleeperi
species.intro: I was keeping Megasoma sleeperi larvae in July 2021. For anyone starting with an egg or a young grub, the most useful comparison I know comes from a southern California series. Van Dam and colleagues followed larvae from eggs laid in captivity and recorded the food that carried three of them to their third instar.

facts.title: Other documented larval food
facts.text: Rotten palo verde wood in captivity

sections.title: The breeders and their young
sections.text: The published brood came from females collected near Glamis in Imperial County, California. The locality consisted of desert drainages with palo verde trees. Adults came to lights between dusk and roughly 11 p.m. The females laid eggs in captivity, which allowed the researchers to link their young to identified adults. I would keep the collection locality with any descendants. Three small North American Megasoma occur in the hobby, and an isolated grub is much harder to identify than a beetle with a documented parent.

sections.title: Choosing a larval food
sections.text: The researchers raised their grubs on mulch made from coast live oak leaves. That oak does not grow at the collection site, making this a particularly useful rearing result. The same paper records larvae feeding on rotten palo verde wood in captivity. The food associated with the adult habitat and the food used in the documented larval series are therefore two distinct options. If I were setting up another group, I would keep the food type with the dates of each observed molt so the brood’s progress could be compared with the published series.

sections.title: Recognizing mature larvae
sections.text: The third-instar description was based on three larvae, with a reported head-capsule width of 6.5 mm. That measurement and the accompanying illustrations are reference points for a grub already known to be this species. I would use an actual molt, where observed, to time the transition between instars.

sources.title: My captive larvae in 2021
Van Dam, Van Dam and Wilcox (2006), captive larval feeding and third-instar description

species.name: Cotinis nitida
species.intro: When green June beetles are flying over open grass, I find it easiest to intercept them in flight. The adults are conspicuous by day. One adult I photographed on the ground shows the green back and pale golden margins along the wing covers.

sections.title: Finding adults
sections.text: I recommend watching the open space just above the grass. Adult activity is easier to follow there than among the leaves of a tree. In a discussion of baits I suggested that banana mixed with wine might also attract Cotinis. My recommendation was based on how easily the beetles can be met in open flight. I did not establish a catch rate for that bait.

sections.title: Eggs, overwintering and emergence
sections.text: In North Carolina, females choose soil rich in organic matter and lay clusters of about 10–30 eggs. Hatching takes roughly two weeks. Grubs feed in the soil and may surface at night. They spend winter underground as larvae. Following spring pupation, adults develop in about two to three weeks. I use those published field intervals as seasonal reference points. The adult in the photograph is a field observation.

facts.title: Personal record
facts.text: Adult field photograph and field-collecting recommendation

facts.title: Published timing
facts.text: About two weeks to hatch and two to three weeks as a pupa in North Carolina

species.name: Euphoria sepulcralis
species.intro: I photographed this small, mottled flower scarab between my fingertips. The body and wing covers are visible together, and the hand gives a sense of the adult’s size. My own record covers the adult stage.

sections.title: Seasonal observations
sections.text: Published records give a useful starting point for looking for a wild brood. In Kentucky the species has an annual life cycle. Pupation was recorded in August, with adults active from late summer into autumn and again the following spring. Florida records span much more of the year. When following adults in different parts of the range, I keep the locality with the date so that the seasonal records remain comparable.

sections.title: Larval habitat
sections.text: Larvae have been found in soil beneath dead sod or manure. That habitat is quite different from the exposed flowers where adults are often encountered. If checking for immature stages, I would look in the organic soil below the dead plant material and keep its origin with any larval observation.

species.name: Euphoria verticalis
species.intro: I photographed a pinned adult of this dark flower scarab with its specimen label. I use this specimen as an adult comparison. The label and the beetle are visible together in the photograph.

sections.title: Comparing adults
sections.text: The photograph shows the outline of the beetle from above. Compare the rounded pronotum, the surface of the wing covers and the overall shape together. Orozco’s revision of Euphoria treats E. verticalis in its own species group and provides the comparative basis for identification. A specimen image of this kind is useful for checking an adult determination before assigning the same name to associated immature stages.

species.name: Chalcolepidius lenzi
species.intro: In August 2021 I set up a female Chalcolepidius lenzi in a ventilated gallon tub. I was keeping a female Chalcolepidius smaragdinus at the same time. Each had her own enclosure, which let me keep the two species separate from the start.
species.account_credit: Adult care by Junkai Wang

facts.title: Container
facts.text: One US gallon (3.8 L), well ventilated

facts.title: Floor
facts.text: 1.3 in (3.3 cm) of moist coconut fiber with bark flats

sections.title: Setting up the female
sections.text: I gave the female about 1.3 inches (3.3 cm) of moist coconut fiber. I laid flat pieces of bark on top. They gave her a place to rest and something to push against when she landed on her back. If I repeated the trial, I would arrange the bark so I could lift a single piece and examine its underside while leaving the rest in place.

sections.title: Where I would look for eggs
sections.text: My 2021 setup documents how I housed an adult. For a breeding attempt, my closest comparison is Chalcolepidius webbi. In that species Alan found eggs on bark or paper towel and reared the larvae individually. I would inspect those surfaces as well as the coir before replacing anything in a lenzi enclosure. I have no egg count or reared adult to assign to my 2021 female.

sections.title: Comparing the adults
sections.text: When identifying another female, I would examine the antennae in addition to the body color. Casari describes the female antennae of C. lenzi as saw-toothed, with stronger teeth in the male. I keep locality and species labels with the enclosure because colors can vary in this genus.

species.name: Chalcolepidius smaragdinus
species.intro: I kept an adult female Chalcolepidius smaragdinus in August 2021. The first decisions were simple ones: enough ventilation, a moist floor, and pieces of bark that a long-bodied adult could use to get back on her feet.
species.account_credit: Adult care by Junkai Wang

facts.title: Container
facts.text: One US gallon (3.8 L), well ventilated

facts.title: Floor
facts.text: 1.3 in (3.3 cm) of moist coconut fiber with bark flats

sections.title: My holding enclosure
sections.text: I used a one-gallon tub, about 3.8 liters, with good ventilation and roughly 1.3 inches (3.3 cm) of moist coconut fiber. I laid bark flats on the surface. My C. lenzi female had the same arrangement in a separate tub. Bark with an accessible underside would let me check for eggs without having to sift all the coir.

sections.title: Planning a laying trial
sections.text: My account for this female ends at adult housing. For another attempt, I would offer both pieces of bark and folded paper towel. In our Chalcolepidius webbi culture, both materials received eggs. I would mark the date when I first saw eggs and the date the young actually hatched. The approximately one-year rearing period we recorded for webbi is a comparison for keeping those records, not a measured duration for smaragdinus.

sections.title: Recognizing southwestern material
sections.text: Casari recorded this species from Arizona, New Mexico and Sonora. The museum type series includes an Arizona specimen from the Gila Valley. The beetle’s metallic appearance comes from scale-like hairs. I would keep a close dorsal photograph with the locality when documenting new material, because both the color and stripes vary among adults.

species.name: Bolitotherus cornutus
species.intro: I would build this setup around an intact shelf fungus. The bracket is the adults’ feeding and courtship site, the female’s laying surface and the food the young tunnel into. My photograph shows the rough, knobbly adult that hides against the surface of its host.

facts.title: Host fungi
facts.text: Ganoderma applanatum, Ganoderma tsugae and Fomes fomentarius

facts.title: Egg hatch
facts.text: About 16 days on average in published observations

facts.title: Pupation
facts.text: Inside the same type of bracket in which the larva feeds

sections.title: Choosing the fungus
sections.text: I would favor a piece of host wood with a living bracket still attached. In their field study, Fornof and colleagues counted more egg-laying events on brackets with living growth. Large brackets drew more adult visits and courtship, but size alone did not predict where females laid. Give the beetles access to the underside as well as the upper surface. Adults commonly shelter under bark or in the fungus by day and come onto the surface after dark.

sections.title: Recognizing a pair
sections.text: A male carries two forward-projecting horns on the segment behind the head, often with conspicuous yellow hairs underneath. A female has two low bumps there. During courtship the male climbs onto her facing the opposite way. This can last minutes to hours. A male can also remain with the female for several hours after mating, so a mounted pair seen on two successive checks could be the same encounter.

sections.title: Following eggs through emergence
sections.text: Look on the bracket itself for individual eggs covered with a dark secretion. I would mark the position on a photograph and leave the covering in place. A hatchling bores directly into the fungal tissue. Four larval instars were observed in laboratory rearings. Pupation also occurs inside the bracket. Keeping occupied brackets intact makes it possible to connect a later emergence with the eggs laid there. Some beetles reach adulthood by late summer. Many overwinter as larvae and appear the following summer, so I would retain a bracket through winter even after adults have disappeared from its surface.

species.name: Eleodes goryi
species.intro: I would start with an identified group of adults and keep its young together by locality. I photographed the glossy black adult on my palm, which gives a sense of its size. A laboratory series from southern Texas shows that this species can lay readily in captivity, but many individuals were lost before their second larval instar.

facts.title: Early survival
facts.text: 25 of 460 eggs and larvae reached the second instar or beyond in the published series

sections.title: Setting up a laying group
sections.text: Smith, Dornburg and Wheeler housed their wild-collected adults in plastic containers with sand. They kept different species, localities and collecting dates separate. I would follow that arrangement, especially with several similar-looking Eleodes in the collection. The researchers sifted each enclosure at intervals of one to two weeks and recovered both eggs and small larvae. Keeping the siftings from each date in a separate container gives a useful age window, even when individual eggs are hard to see.

sections.title: Feeding and moisture below the surface
sections.text: The young were raised in a mixture of sand and food. To maintain moisture the study used either daily watering or a plaster base supplied with water through a short tube. The latter establishes a gradient from the bottom up. I would keep one corner available for checking the damp layer and observe where the young settle. The study pooled its description of the rearing methods across several species, so it does not establish which watering method gave the best survival for this particular stock.

sections.title: Recognizing a growing larva
sections.text: The published account followed 460 eggs and larvae from adults collected at Bentsen–Rio Grande Valley State Park. Only 25 reached the second instar or later. I would therefore count young again after their first molt before judging the success of a laying group. Late larvae have conspicuously darker dorsal plates on the eighth and ninth abdominal segments. These were useful in separating them from the other Eleodes larvae in the study. The illustrated descriptions were based on larvae in roughly their eighth through eleventh instars.

species.name: Cryptoglossa variolosa
species.intro: I photographed two adult Cryptoglossa variolosa together on weathered wood. For a first enclosure I would pay particular attention to the ground and the refuges beneath it. The published records are strongest on habitat, defensive behavior and identification of the young.

facts.title: Documented habitat
facts.text: Arid southwestern North America, including the Sand Tank Mountains of Arizona

facts.title: Adult behavior
facts.text: Ground-dwelling, with shelter use and defensive postures documented in the genus

facts.title: Immature stages
facts.text: Described and keyed by Rolf Aalbu in his revision of the tribe

sections.title: Cover and surface activity
sections.text: I would give adults a dry walking surface and low, stable shelters they can reach from more than one side. A piece of bark placed where the beetles can be seen from the side lets me inspect a refuge without dismantling it. Aalbu described retreat into shelter and a head-down defensive posture among Cryptoglossa. An adult disturbed while cover is lifted may also become motionless. I would set the cover back gently and watch the beetle when it resumes walking.

sections.title: Choosing a starting setup
sections.text: The Sand Tank Mountains survey recorded both this species and Cryptoglossa muricata in the same Arizona mountain range. I would keep identified founders in separate groups and retain a photograph of each from above. I watched the two adults on the surface of the wood. For a laying trial I would also give them accessible soil and keep part of it undisturbed.

sections.title: Documenting the young
sections.text: Aalbu’s illustrated treatment includes immature C. variolosa and provides a key to the young of several closely related species. I would use that work together with the identity of the parents if a larva appeared. The most helpful details to retain are the date and location of the first larva in the enclosure, its subsequent molts, and whether an adult ultimately emerges. I have no measured incubation or pupation schedule for these beetles.

species.name: Alaus oculatus
species.intro: The two black spots on the thorax make an adult eastern eyed click beetle easy to notice on a log. The stage that matters most in a rearing enclosure is hidden inside it. The larva is a predator with a large appetite for other beetle larvae.

facts.title: Larval habitat
facts.text: Decaying hardwood, especially stumps of oak, cherry and apple

facts.title: Documented prey
facts.text: Wood-boring beetle larvae, including longhorn grubs

facts.title: Adult identification
facts.text: A black background with large white-rimmed false eyespots on the thorax

sections.title: Setting up adults
sections.text: I would follow my general Alaus setup and provide moist organic material with a textured surface, cover and room for a female to investigate the upper layers. In my family guide I describe eggs laid near the surface and adults accepting jelly or fruit. Those are starting points from work with click beetles. For this species I would also include a piece of softened hardwood, consistent with its recorded larval habitat. When pairing adults, check the spots on the shield behind the head. Each occupies about one-third of the shield’s length in this species. The true eyes are on the head.

sections.title: Feeding an individual larva
sections.text: I would move each hatchling to its own container early and offer appropriately sized invertebrate prey. The wood provides shelter and a place to hunt. In records summarized by R. E. Woodruff, caged larvae each consumed more than 200 longhorn beetle larvae over the course of development. That figure gives a sense of the food needed over a larva’s lifetime. I would use whether the last prey item was taken and the appearance of the larva to decide when to feed again.

sections.title: Identifying a larva from wood
sections.text: A mature larva can approach 5 cm. The body is elongate and hard, with a dark head, prominent jaws and a pair of forked terminal projections. In fallen hardwood I would keep a potential predator away from any wood-feeding longhorn grubs I intend to rear. Alan’s adult photograph and published larval illustrations give two points of comparison when an adult emerges from an individually labeled piece of wood.

sources.title: Alan Jeon’s adult photograph
Junkai Wang, click beetle care in Beetles by Family
Woodruff, click beetles of the genus Alaus and observations of larval feeding

species.name: Alaus myops
species.intro: The small-eyed click beetle has a close association with dead pine. Its larvae follow other insects through the galleries under the bark. H. E. Savely’s study of North Carolina logs records what the young larvae ate and where to look as the wood aged.
species.account_credit: Adult photograph by Alan Jeon · Natural history and care notes by Junkai Wang and Alan Jeon

facts.title: Larval habitat
facts.text: Under bark and inside beetle galleries in dead pine

facts.title: Documented prey
facts.text: Longhorn beetle and fire-colored beetle larvae

facts.title: Autumn observation
facts.text: A pupa and an adult in an approximately two-year-old pine stump in October

sections.title: Recognizing the adult
sections.text: I look at the shield just behind the head. Each dark eyespot on A. myops measures less than a quarter of the shield’s length. Gray scales cover more than half the brown upper surface, giving the beetle the mottled appearance in my adult photograph. The familiar eastern eyed click beetle, A. oculatus, has larger spots, each about a third of the shield’s length, and sparse white scales over black.

sections.title: What the young larvae hunt
sections.text: In pines that had died within the year, Savely found larvae up to about 10–15 mm long. He saw them take the longhorn Acanthocinus obsoletus, the fire-colored beetle Dendroides bicolor and other small larvae. For a young click beetle I would use a piece of pine with some bark still attached and offer small prey where the wood meets the bark. I would house it individually so I could tell what it had eaten.

sections.title: Following a larva through the galleries
sections.text: Savely found larvae as long as 30 mm in second-year pine alongside larvae of 10 mm or less, suggesting females can lay eggs in a log after its first year. In third-year pine he still found them under bark and in tunnels made by longhorns and the darkling beetle Xylopinus rufipes. I would keep an occupied piece intact when adding fresh material, especially if the larva disappears from view in autumn. For a reared animal, I would record its hatch, pupation and emergence dates separately. Savely knew how long each tree had been dead, while the age of an individual beetle inside it could vary.

species.name: Orthosoma brunneum
species.intro: I photographed an adult brown prionid on my hand, where its long antennae and ridged wing covers show clearly. Adults regularly come to lights across eastern North America. For anyone starting with an adult, a damp piece of already decaying wood gives the female a place to lay and the resulting larvae material they can eat for months.
species.account_credit: Adult photograph by Alan Jeon · Natural history and care notes by Junkai Wang and Alan Jeon

facts.title: Egg-laying season
facts.text: May through late summer in Maryland

sections.title: Identifying and feeding adults
sections.text: I would check the shield behind the head for three sharp points on each side and look along the wing covers for the raised parallel lines. Adults are recorded from May through November in the eastern United States. Paula Shrewsbury reports that they feed on flowers, fruit and leaves. With a newly collected adult I would offer a little ripe fruit on a removable dish and check for feeding while the beetle is active.

sections.title: Selecting wood for egg laying
sections.text: The tree species gives the keeper considerable choice. Recorded hardwoods include oak, hickory, walnut, chestnut, maple and basswood. Larvae also develop in pine, hemlock and fir. The feature I would select for first is decay in a piece that still holds moisture. I would set the wood partly into a damp substrate and leave some of its surface accessible. Published observations place eggs on or in decaying wood and sometimes in the surrounding soil, so I would keep that soil with the wood when moving the female.

sections.title: Watching for larvae
sections.text: The pale, glossy larvae can reach about 50 mm. Their tunnels accumulate coarse, fibrous frass. If I exposed one of those galleries, I would leave most of it intact and record the kind of wood and its condition. Allow two to three years for larval development. Laboratory rearers have also raised this species using a formulated diet with host-plant material. That result gives a second rearing option for a keeper who can reproduce the published preparation.

species.name: Embaphion muricatum
species.intro: The upturned rim of this beetle’s back is what first caught my eye. I kept pie-dish beetles in December 2021 and had larvae of Embaphion muricatum available by March 2022. In 2024 Alan reared a fresh group to its first adult. The young are slender soil-dwellers, quite unlike the broad, shallow-dished adults.

facts.title: Our stock
facts.text: Larvae in March 2022, new adult in July 2024

facts.title: Successful substrate
facts.text: About 3 in (7.5 cm) of ReptiSoil mixed with excavator clay

facts.title: Pupation site
facts.text: An earthen cell below the surface

sections.title: A substrate that produced an adult
sections.text: Alan’s account from July 2024: I received fresh stock earlier that year and set it up in a gasket-sealed tub. I mixed ReptiSoil with excavator clay and gave the beetles about three inches (7.5 cm) of this mixture. I did not add rotten wood. On July 10 I saw the first adult from that group. This is the setup I would start with for another batch of pie-dish larvae.

sections.title: Starting with adults
sections.text: I would give the adults cover they can walk under and a bed of diggable soil deep enough for the larvae to disappear into it. My Eleodes hispilabris setup offers one way to arrange a darkling enclosure. For pie-dish beetles I would leave a slightly damp area below the surface so a full-grown larva can form a cell that holds its shape. I would keep the feeding area accessible for checks without turning over the whole enclosure.

sections.title: Feeding the larvae
sections.text: Wheat, hulless oats and rye are useful foods to start with. Both adults and larvae accepted seeds in laboratory feeding trials. I would offer a small amount at a recognizable spot and check the grains as well as the soil beneath them. A larva can eat into a seed from below while leaving little sign at the surface.

sections.title: Following pupation
sections.text: Once I have larger larvae, I would leave part of the bed undisturbed and check through the side of the container. The finished cell is fragile, so I would wait for the adult to leave it before moving the beetle. In Kansas both larvae and adults have been found overwintering. My March 2022 larvae establish which stage I had that spring, but the interval after my December account is not a measured egg-to-larva time.

species.name: Thylodrias contractus
species.intro: I started my odd beetle culture with about 30 living larvae that I recovered from a damaged insect collection in February 2026. The beetles were especially common around moths and orthopterans. By mid-March several had matured. Two months later I nearly wrote the culture off before I spotted the tiny larvae of the next generation.

sections.title: Moving the larvae
sections.text: I first look beneath damaged specimens and in the loose debris around them. That was where I could recover living larvae among the remains. For a new colony I would move some of the material on which the larvae have already been feeding to a separate, close-fitting container. I considered crickets as a substitute for the dried insects. The damage I actually observed was to moths and orthopterans in the collection. I keep a live culture well away from pinned specimens.

sections.title: Recognizing adults of both sexes
sections.text: An adult female can look so much like a larva that it is easy to overlook her during a count. Females are wingless throughout adult life. Males have wing covers, but the hind wings underneath vary considerably in size. I look for both forms when checking for maturity, then use the appearance of a new size class of small larvae as evidence of reproduction.

sections.title: When the enclosure looks empty
sections.text: Several larvae had matured during the two weeks before my March 15 check. On May 19, small larvae finally caught my eye in the enclosure. I would keep an apparently quiet container and examine the remaining food under magnification before starting over. A laboratory study found a typical life cycle of 12.8 months, with individuals ranging from about six and a half months to more than 46 months. My February founders were already larvae when I collected them, so their March emergence tells me when the first adults appeared, but not their total age.

species.name: Dermestes marmoratus
species.intro: Of the four or so Dermestes species I had seen by August 2025, this was the largest. My beetles began breeding in their temporary enclosure. I photographed an adult in September. Its mottled wing covers make a good field mark to look for when checking which species has established in a box.

facts.text: 9–13 mm in the North American identification key

sections.title: Starting a colony
sections.text: I would begin with a small amount of dry animal material and leave the group together. The food history of this species gives me a better starting point than a fruit or jelly feeder. Its published records include carrion and accumulations of dead insects. I would supply a separate piece of dry material to lift when I check the box so I can find young larvae without disturbing the whole group.

sections.title: Checking the holding box
sections.text: My first breeding result came while the group was still in temporary housing. For that reason I check the food, loose debris and sheltered edges before moving the adults into a permanent setup. Small larvae can remain behind when the conspicuous adults have all been transferred. I keep this colony separate from the dry insects in my specimen collection.

sections.title: Recognizing the adults
sections.text: Under good light I look for a marbled pattern of dark and pale hairs on the wing covers. A paler band extends inward from behind each shoulder. Several North American Dermestes are mottled, so I use the identification key when starting with new field material. The September photograph shows the appearance of my own adult.

species.name: Gibbium aequinoctiale
species.intro: My smooth spider beetles were slow to establish. In July 2024, around two years after I remembered starting the culture, I counted roughly 30 adults. I had raised Mezium affine on the same food, and that colony built up much sooner. The two are similar enough in the hand that I like to compare them under magnification.

sections.title: Feeding and checking the colony
sections.text: I used dog food for both of my spider beetle species. With Gibbium I also considered trying oats and artificial pollen. The food I can recommend from my own breeding result is dog food. I would offer it in small pieces that I can lift and inspect, and keep the crumbs in the culture until I have checked them for tiny beetles. A close-fitting lid and fine ventilation are worthwhile with adults this small.

sections.title: Allowing for a slow start
sections.text: By my July 21 check I could see about 30 adults. The culture took roughly three times as long to get established as my Mezium affine. The adults seemed short-lived to me, although I could not tell whether a delay during the egg or larval stage accounted for the slow buildup. I use the two-year figure to describe the history of my colony. It does not represent the developmental time of an individual. I once thought I had lost the culture because I could hardly find adults during the day. A night check showed they were still active.

sections.title: Telling my two cultures apart
sections.text: I check the head and the narrow shield just behind it. Both are smooth in Gibbium, as are the shiny, swollen wing covers. In Mezium affine, the head and shield have conspicuous pale hairs. These are widespread spider beetles associated with stored materials and found in North America. I label each culture before moving food or beetles between containers.

species.name: Mezium affine
species.intro: I bred this small, round spider beetle on dog food. Of the two spider beetles I kept, Mezium affine was the quicker to build into an established colony. Its polished wing covers look much like those of Gibbium aequinoctiale, but a hand lens shows that the front of the body is covered in hairs.

sections.title: Care and feeding
sections.text: I use the same staple food that worked for my Gibbium colony. I would keep small portions of dog food in a secure container and check the food and crumbs together. I use a pale tray for looking through a small sample. Against a light surface it is easier to see the tiny, reddish-brown adults move away from the food. Before replacing the bottom material, I would keep a portion with the established group. In October 2025 I found grain mites in my Mezium culture. Since both can be present in the crumbs, I would check them under magnification before moving material to a fresh box.

sections.title: Following the colony
sections.text: I compare the numbers of adults I can see at successive checks. My Mezium became established substantially sooner than the Gibbium, which took roughly three times as long to build up. That comparison is about the time it took my cultures to become productive. I did not follow a single egg through to adulthood in that comparison.

sections.title: Recognizing the species
sections.text: For a quick comparison, I look immediately behind the head. A coat of pale hairs covers the head and pronotum, while the much larger wing covers have a glossy surface. I check those characters before transferring beetles between cultures. The species occurs in North America and elsewhere in stored animal and plant products, which fits its readiness to use dog food in my care.

species.name: Zopherus nodulosus
species.intro: The Texas ironclads in my enclosure gathered on lichen and fed readily. I keep the black-and-white Texas form, Zopherus nodulosus haldemani. In my latest breeding trial I changed how I arranged the wood, standing spent mushroom logs upright to give the beetles access to the sides as well as the ends.

sections.title: Feeding the adults
sections.text: I offer lichen on its supporting bark so I can see where the beetles have been feeding. In the photograph, several adults are gathered on the same piece. For another group I would keep a feeding surface accessible at the front of the enclosure.

sections.title: The upright-log trial
sections.text: For my November 2026 setup I stacked spent mushroom logs vertically. I wanted to see whether wood already worked by the fungus would support the larvae. I would keep the logs stable while checking the adults and retain any piece that shows signs of tunnelling. Feeding was the result I had confirmed when I photographed the setup. I was still waiting to rear larvae from the wood.

species.name: Dorcus brevis
species.intro: My first broods of Dorcus brevis grew to the third instar and then died. Getting eggs was only the first part of the problem. I kept working with this species and eventually raised it through the adult molt. In January 2021 I photographed one of my captive-bred adults.

sections.title: Selecting a pair
sections.text: Check the adults against Dorcus parallelus before pairing them. Viewed from above, the rear corners of the pronotum lie close to the bases of the wing covers in D. brevis. A small male can have short jaws and a narrow head. The shape of the mandibles is more useful than jaw length alone for deciding whether a beetle is female. I have seen a small male mistaken for a newly emerged female on just those grounds.

sections.title: Laying and larval development
sections.text: For a pair I recommend a piece of decaying hardwood embedded in less-fermented hardwood flake soil, the general Dorcus setup described on the Substrate page. Offer active adults beetle jelly every five days, with apple or banana as alternatives. My early attempts produced larvae repeatedly, but they died during the third instar. By the time I was setting up my third attempt in 2014, I suspected that the larvae might need a seasonal rest. I had no tested chilling temperature or duration.

sections.title: Recognizing success
sections.text: For any repeat of this culture I recommend recording three dates separately, when the larva last fed, when a pupa became visible and when the adult molted. The captive-bred adult I later photographed establishes that this species can complete its development in culture. I did not establish which change allowed the successful brood to pass the stage where my earlier broods failed.

species.name: Platycerus oregonensis
species.intro: One pair of Oregon stag beetles produced approximately 13 larvae for me. One of those grubs spent months pale and motionless after constructing a chamber. It looked ready to pupate, but by the following March it had resumed feeding as a larva.

sections.title: Rearing the brood
sections.text: The larvae grew well at first. During summer the room repeatedly became hot, and all but one of the young beetles died. The survivor reached the third instar. My experience is a reason to pay attention to the warmest temperature in the rearing room, especially in a place that stays comfortable for most of the day but heats up for a few hours. I did not measure a maximum safe temperature. If repeating the setup, I would choose a place with less summer heat and keep pieces of the food wood with each feeding grub.

sections.title: Watching a resting larva
sections.text: As the room cooled after summer, the survivor made a chamber. Its gut emptied and the body became visibly pale. I initially expected a pupa and waited for several months. When I checked in March, I could again see brown wood in its gut, and the larva had a bluish cast while it fed. From this one animal I learned to leave a quiet third instar and its chamber intact. An empty gut can precede a long pause followed by renewed feeding. Look for the actual pupal molt before marking that stage in your records.

species.name: Sinodendron rugosum
species.intro: I tried breeding this small western stag beetle in both pieces of decaying wood and flake soil. The females readily bored into the logs. By the end of the trial I had found no larvae in either setup. A gallery was the clearest sign I saw of adult activity, but it was insufficient to establish a brood.

sections.title: Adults in wood
sections.text: These beetles reminded me of bess beetles in the way they worked into the wood. The adults appeared to eat it, although watching them excavate a tunnel could not tell me how much they actually swallowed. For another trial, I would keep intact pieces of wood available so the adults could continue boring and I could follow the occupied pieces separately.

sections.title: What to try in a subsequent culture
sections.text: Wood species is one variable worth changing. Furniss and colleagues recorded this species emerging from decaying alder collected at Sheep Creek in Idaho. That gives me a specific wood to try and a reason to keep a note of its type and state of decay. In my earlier setups I saw females drill into logs, but I never found eggs or grubs to connect with those tunnels. For a repeat I would leave each occupied piece intact, check any loose material around it for young larvae, and record the first hatchling separately from the first sign of adult drilling.

facts.title: Outcome
facts.text: No larvae recovered in either setup

species.name: Ceruchus piceus
species.intro: I photographed this small eastern stag beetle in the field. A decaying log can hold several stages of its life cycle, which makes the wood itself an important part of any attempt to keep it. My photograph documents an adult. The rearing suggestions below draw on its known habitat.

sections.title: Recognizing adults
sections.text: The body is glossy and black to dark reddish brown. Adult body length is approximately 10–14 mm without the mandibles. In males, look for the enlarged mandibles and a prominent tooth on the inner edge. I recommend photographing the beetle from above before it disappears back into a crevice. The mandibles and the outline of the head can then be checked together.

sections.title: Choosing wood
sections.text: Published records include decaying logs of beech, birch, black cherry, oak and red pine. When selecting material for a trial, I would start with the species and condition of the wood in which the beetle was found. Keep some intact sections as well as loose decayed wood. A field account from the Université de Montréal describes pupation within a decomposing stump. If you encounter an occupied chamber, leave the surrounding walls in place and inspect only where the cell is already visible. I have a field record for this species and no measured egg-to-adult interval from my own culture.

species.name: Platycerus quercus
species.intro: I photographed an adult oak stag beetle small enough to rest on the palm of my hand. This is a field account. Decaying oak is a sensible starting point for working with the species, and spring records give a useful indication of when adults may be active.

sections.title: Where to look for adults
sections.text: Look in the crevices of decaying logs and under loose bark. Adult oak stag beetles have also been collected on blackberry flowers. In Maryland, Staines and Staines recorded two specimens in a funnel trap between April 5 and 13. Those captures provide a local example of early adult activity. I would check both the wood and the vegetation nearby when following a population through spring.

sections.title: Wood for a rearing trial
sections.text: For a first trial I would retain a section of the occupied log and keep the softer, partly crumbled material in contact with it. Larvae attributed to the oak stag beetle have been reported feeding in decaying oak logs and stumps. The adults found on blossoms and the larvae feeding in wood use different parts of the habitat. An adult on a flower alone gives no information about the wood that supported it as a grub. My adult photograph documents the field identification. I do not have a brood count or a measured developmental interval for this species.

sections.title: Beetle Substrate Guide
sections.subtitle: Lets make this as easy as possible
paragraphs: Here are the very basics: in regards to US native species, Dynastes tityus and granti, Strategus aloeus and antaeus, Gymnetis thula and any Cotinis species, Osmoderma species and Euphoria species can be raised on "Organic Raised Bed Soil" alone! If a larger size is desired, simply mix in raw sawdust! This will be explained in the next slide. But without any mixtures, the organic soil alone will achieve average sized adult beetles!

sections.title: Mixing the Organic Raised Bed Soil
sections.subtitle: Say goodbye to hard to make flake soil!
paragraphs: So if you decide to go down the dark path of ditching flake soil once and for all, but still want that sweet large major male, know that it is still very doable, and easy! Mix in 3/10th of the substrate mass in raw sawdust, you can use any of the hardwood grilling pellets consisting of Oak or Mesquite wood. I personally opt for Mesquite as it is the most affordable option. Make sure the sawdust expands and stir it with the "Organic Raised Bed Soil" throughly. Leave the mixture for two weeks, and stir it whenever you remember to do so (doesn't have to be often). Once the two weeks is up, it is ready for you to add beetles!

A. make sure the organic soil you use do not compose of cow manure. Cow manure contains a bacteria that can cause leg rot with a lot of beetle larvae species and can kill your larvae quickly. That said, most "Organic Raised Bed Soil" purchased from Walmart or Home Depot does not contain cow manure and can be used without issues.
B. This substrate mix is not meant for: any US Lucanid (stag beetles), and any of them Phileurus or Hemiphileurus species.
C. If the intent is to raise large cetoniids (flower beetles), adding a large portion of rotting leaves will also yield desirable results, although raw sawdust works perfectly fine.

sections.title: Making Flake Soil
sections.subtitle: You gotta do it sometime
paragraphs: You really don't have to stress about making flake soil - things ferment in the wild all without human intervention after all. But sometimes, we just gotta speed it up!

sections.title: How to Make Flake Soil
sections.subtitle: Can't be that hard can it?
paragraphs: First up - if you leave raw sawdust by itself in a moist state long enough, certain lucanids will eat it. Yes, you heard me right, the more hardy species will do just fine on aged sawdust. But this might cost you 6 months - a year's time.
So, how do you make flake soil?

Well, you will need ingredients first. 20lbs of hardwood grilling pellets of just about any brand will do the trick for the wood part, but oak and mesquite are your best choices. Then, you need to add 7.5lbs of unbleached flour, and some dry yeast.
The first step is to pour out and expand the pellets with water, and then turn it into sawdust. Warm water works best with this step, but cold will do just fine.

Then you pour the flour into the expanded pellets, along with a table spoon of yeast. You want to mix throughly here, so there isn't huge clumps of flour - an occasional small piece here and there is fine.

The end result should be damp, but not wet. You can check it by squeezing the substrate. It should form a clump and not fall apart when released, all the while having no water come out. If you made it too wet, leave it in somewhere sunny for a few days and stir more often, you will be fine.

Now the waiting game begins. In this stage, you want to mix up the substrate at least once in 2 days (once a day is better). You should notice the substrate heating up, if it does not heat up, simply add more yeast.
It will be about 3 weeks to a month before the soil is ready. Be sure to wait till the substrate is fully cooled down.
Yay, now you have flake soil! The rest of beetle keeping will be a breeze!
